title: What should you say at each stage of a case interview?
description: The phrases strong candidates use at each of the ten stages of a case interview, from the first recap to the final recommendation.
hook: At each stage of a case you have one job, and one or two sentences that do it: confirm the goal, ask what changes your plan, lay out a structure, propose the next step, turn each number into a so-what, and finish with a clear answer. This guide gives you a line for every one of the ten stages, then shows them working together in one short case.
body:
In this guide

  • The ten stages at a glance
  • Stages 1 to 3: listen, recap, clarify
  • Stage 4: present your structure
  • Stages 5 to 7: lead, read charts, do the maths
  • Stages 8 to 10: brainstorm, recommend, and the habits in between
  • One case, start to finish
  • Common mistakes
  • Practise the lines
  • Where to practise next

The ten stages at a glance

Most cases follow the same arc, whether the interviewer leads you through set questions or expects you to steer.

StageYour job
1. ListenCapture the goal
2. RecapConfirm the problem
3. ClarifyAsk what changes your plan
4. StructureLay out the plan and a hypothesis
5. LeadPropose the next step
6. ChartsFind the insight
7. MathsApproach, calculate, check
8. BrainstormIdeas in buckets
9. RecommendAnswer first
10. ThroughoutLink back to the goal

Stages 1 to 3: listen, recap, clarify

The opening is the most predictable part of any case, so it is where prepared lines help most. The full method is in how to open a case in the first two minutes.

Listen

Write the goal at the top of your page, with its number and deadline. Mark anything unclear and ask when the interviewer finishes.

"Before I recap, one quick check: when you said contribution, did you mean contribution per order?"
"Interesting that revenue fell while volume held. I may want to come back to price."

Recap

Client, problem, measurable goal, then a check. Three sentences at most, never the prompt read back.

"So our client is X, facing Y, and success means Z by [date]. Did I get that right?"

Clarify

Ask only the questions whose answers would change your structure, usually two or three. Then ask for time.

"How does the client actually make money?"
"Is this happening across the industry, or just to our client?"
"Thank you, that's useful. May I take a moment to structure my thoughts?"

Stage 4: present your structure

Big points first, numbered, then say where you would start and why. A hypothesis shows you are solving the problem, not just organising it. More on building the tree itself in how to structure your answer.

"There are three areas I want to look at: revenue, costs and the market. I suspect the problem is on the cost side, because revenue has grown, so I'd start there."

Stages 5 to 7: lead, read charts, do the maths

Lead

After every answer, say what you want to look at next, what data you need and why. In interviewer-led cases, which are common at McKinsey, the interviewer chooses the next question, but saying where you would go still shows judgement. See how to drive a case.

"As a next step, I'd like to check whether the decline is industry-wide. Do we have market data?"

Charts

Ask for a moment, read the title, axes, units and footnotes, then give insights rather than a description.

"Thank you. May I take a moment to read this?"
"Two things stand out. First... Second... Given our goal, the second matters more, and I'd like to size it."

Maths

State the approach before any arithmetic, talk through the calculation, then sanity-check the result and say what it means.

"My approach: market size × our share × margin gives yearly profit, which I'd compare with the investment to get the payback. Does that sound right before I run the numbers?"
"Quick sanity check: 2M units at $50 is $100M, which is 20% of a $500M market. Plausible for a leader."

Stages 8 to 10: brainstorm, recommend, and the habits in between

Brainstorm

Name your buckets first, fill them, then pick a priority.

"Let me think about this in two buckets: what we can do with today's capabilities, and what needs new ones."

Recommend

Answer first, two or three reasons with numbers, the main risk, next steps. Put any branch you did not reach into the next steps. The full method is in how to give a strong recommendation.

"I recommend entering through a joint venture. Two reasons: the market grows 12% a year, and a partner caps our investment at $20M. The key risk is depending on the partner, so as next steps I'd agree exit terms and test demand in one city."

Throughout

Every finding should end with why it matters for the goal you wrote at the top of the page. If you get lost, step back out loud rather than going quiet (practice question 3 below shows how).

"...and this matters because our client's goal is to get back to $3M of contribution."

One case, start to finish

Here is how the lines fit together in a short, illustrative case. The interviewer says: "A regional delivery company is handling more deliveries than ever, but its contribution has fallen. The CEO wants to know why and what to do."

Recap and clarify. "So volume is growing but contribution is falling, and we need the cause and a fix. Did I get that right? Is there a target, and has the customer base changed this year?" The goal is to get back to last year's contribution, and the company has signed a large marketplace contract.

Structure. "I'd split contribution into volume and contribution per delivery, then look at each by customer group. Given the new contract, my hypothesis is that it carries a lower margin, so I'd start with contribution per delivery by customer."

Maths and so-what. The interviewer shares the numbers: last year 1.0M deliveries at $3.00 of contribution each, so $3.0M. This year 1.2M deliveries at an average of $2.00, so $2.4M. "Volume is up 20%, but contribution is down $0.6M. Volume on its own added 0.2M × $3 = $0.6M, while the $1 fall in contribution per delivery cost 1.2M × $1 = $1.2M. So the problem is unit economics, not volume."

Lead. "Next I'd like to split that $2.00 average between existing customers and the new contract. Do we have that?" The data: existing customers 1.0M deliveries at $2.60, so $2.6M; the new contract 0.2M deliveries at minus $1.00, so minus $0.2M. Together, $2.4M.

Insight. "Two things are happening. Every new-contract delivery loses $1, and costs on the core business have risen by $0.40 a delivery, which is worth $0.4M a year. The second is the bigger problem."

Recommend. "I recommend two moves. Reprice or exit the marketplace contract, which recovers $0.2M, and find the $0.40 cost increase on core deliveries, worth $0.4M, starting with driver and fuel costs. Together they take us back to $3.0M. The main risk is losing the marketplace's future volume, so as a next step I'd test whether it will accept a higher rate before we walk away."

Every sentence above does one of four jobs: it asks for evidence, interprets it, proposes a next step or answers the question. Record three minutes of a practice case, label each sentence that way, and cut the ones that do none of them.

Common mistakes

  • Reciting lines word for word. Interviewers hear the same stock phrases all day. Keep the job of each line and change the words.
  • Describing instead of interpreting. "Revenue fell 8%" is a fact. "Revenue fell 8% while volume held, so price or mix is the issue" is an insight. See so-what thinking.
  • Ending answers with "Where would you like me to go next?" Propose a next step instead, and accept a redirect gracefully.

Practise the lines

Say each answer out loud before you open it.

1. The interviewer finishes the prompt with "...and the client wants to grow." There is no number. What do you say?

Show the answer

Recap, then ask for the goal: "So our client wants to grow, and we need to find the best way to do it. Is there a specific growth target, and by when?" A quantified goal is what you link every later answer back to.

2. You have just calculated that a new product would add $4M of profit a year. Finish the thought.

Show the answer

Sanity-check and link to the goal: "So about $4M a year. If the target is $10M, that closes 40% of the gap, so we'd need at least one more lever. Next I'd like to look at..." The number only matters once you compare it with something.

3. You are halfway through and realise you have lost the thread. What do you say?

Show the answer

"Let me take a step back. We know revenue is flat and costs rose in two lines. We're trying to restore profit, so the next thing to check is which of those two lines we can actually change." Calm, out loud, and it ends with a next step.

Where to practise next

Each stage has its own explainer, starting with what to do while the interviewer reads the case. To drill the lines until they come naturally, use the flashcards on the perfect casing page. Then run a full case from the casebook, such as Coastal Brew, out loud, and check yourself against the most common case interview mistakes.
